claims.claim: On the second day Luther waited at the emperor's court from after four until six o'clock, 'almost smothered for the press'
The evening of the second hearing was 18 April 1521
Köstlin, as cited by Luther's 1930 editors, dates Luther's Worms speech to 18 April 1521
The second hearing was on the day after the first
Luther's own account: 'Then they gave me one day and one night'
The Diet's own record, the Deutsche Reichstagsakten, is cited by Mirbt as his source for the Edict
Foxe names his sources for the Worms account: Melanchthon's history, Sleidan, the Ursperg chronicle's continuation and another (name damaged in the OCR)
Pallavicino says he found matters in the letters of Girolamo Aleander, sent to Germany by the pope on Luther's business
Pallavicino says Aleander reported to Rome on the news of Luther's disappearance
Pallavicino's history is the 1664 revised edition; the first appeared in 1656-1657
The emperor ordered 'a sitting or assembly of the states of all the empire' at Worms for 6 January 1521, and it began that day
The Edict names those present as the empire's 'churfürsten, fürsten und stende jetzo hie versamelt'
Sarpi gives the Edict as saying the herald was sent 'not to know and judge the things that concern Faith, which belongeth to the Pope alone'
Exsurge Domine is dated 15 June 1520
Mirbt summarizes the bull's sentence: penalties for Luther and his followers unless they recanted within 60 days of its publication
Luther burned the bull at Wittenberg on 10 December 1520
Aleander held that a notorious heretic already sentenced by the pope ought not to be heard, and that no safe-conduct was owed
Waterworth: Aleander 'was indeed averse to this summons'
The estates warned that violent measures would 'call forth the greatest commotion' and asked for 'merely ... a summary interrogatory'
The estates' draft grievances say 'achtet man von nöten, das derhalben ain besserung und gemain reformation geschehe'
Buchheim: the estates presented their gravamina to Charles, with the approval of George, duke of Saxony
Frederick asked the legates that Luther's error 'might first be known, before he were made a heretic'
Foxe says Leo sent two legates to Frederick, Aleander one of them
Waterworth: Frederick said the cited works could not, he was persuaded, be from Luther's pen
Luther would recant only if convinced by Scripture and probable reasons
Luther's own account: 'God's Word is not my word, therefore I know not how to give it away'
Charles cited Luther on 6 March 'through the instigation of duke Frederic'
Frederick declined to summon Luther; the citation of 6 March 1521 came in the name of emperor and estates, with a safe-conduct
Luther: 'On Tuesday in the Passion week ... I was cited by the herald'
Luther names the emperor and the electors in person at his hearing
The three spiritual electors were at Worms, by Luther's Table Talk
Albrecht of Mainz signed the ban as head of the Diet
Joachim of Brandenburg spoke to Luther in the talks
Present at the talks: the archbishop of Trier, Joachim of Brandenburg, George of Saxony, the bishops of Augsburg and Brandenburg, Bock of Strasbourg, Peutinger and Dr. Voeus
Frederick of Saxony was at Worms and spoke before the three spiritual electors, by Luther's account
Lewis, elector Palatine, opposed breaking faith with Luther
Philip of Hesse, 'then but a young Prince', said 'is your cause just and upright, then I beseech God to assist you'
Caracciolo and Aleander were at the emperor's residence for the ban, with Mainz and the cardinal of Sion at the signing
Schurff, a Wittenberg lawyer, asked that the titles of the books be read
Schurff asked that the titles be read, by Luther's own account
Caspar Sturm, the emperor's herald, conducted Luther from Wittenberg to Worms
Sturm overtook Luther at Oppenheim to conduct him home
Luther came with perhaps a hundred horse and entered Worms with only eight
Waterworth gives a hundred horsemen and only eight mounted attendants
About twenty-five of Luther's books lay before him
'The books lay on a table which he showed unto me'
Cochlaeus offered to dispute if Luther yielded up his safe-conduct
Glapion ('Sglapian'), the emperor's confessor, had Bucer warn Luther at Oppenheim not to enter Worms
Justus Jonas went with Luther to Worms, by the note of Crespin's editors
Luther arrived at Worms on 16 April
Herrnschmid: 'He came thither, April 16' (the held OCR gives his name as 'John Daniel Hernnfehmid', arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.3492)
Foxe: Luther entered Worms 'about seventeen days after Easter'
Eck's two questions: whether the books were Luther's, and 'Whether thou wilt recant and revoke them'
Luther owned the books and asked for time to deliberate
Luther owned the books and asked 'respite of time', by his own account
At the first hearing Charles said 'Costui certamente non mi farebbe mai diventar' Eretico' (OCR: 'Cq^/w cerramaue non mi farebbe mai dinentar' Eretico')
Waterworth: 'This man at least would never make me a heretic'
Luther's plain answer: 'I will not, nor may not revoke any manner of thing ... Hereupon I stand and rest: I have not what else to say. God have mercy upon me!'
Spaniards jeered at Luther on his way to his lodging after the second hearing

On the morning of 19 April Charles declared in a French document in his own hand. He would maintain what his ancestors adopted, 'more especially at the Council of Constance'. He would not hear Luther again

Charles brought before the electors and princes a paper in his own hand, a full sheet long, later read in consistory at Rome. The held OCR ('£ « legger') leaves unclear whether he read it himself or had it read. He would hear Luther no more and would proceed against him 'come notorio eretico'
Foxe gives the emperor's letter 'in effect' on the Friday following: 'we will not violate our faith, which we have promised him'
Pallavicino: 'Tutta la Dieta concorse nella sentenza di Cesare'
Some at the Diet held, after Constance, that faith need not be kept; the elector Palatine opposed them
The archbishop of Trier met Luther on the morrow after St George's day, with other princes
Pallavicino names the archbishop of Trier who undertook to persuade Luther as Richard Greiffenklau (held OCR 'Riccardo Grieffeclau'), a close friend of Frederick but a good Catholic
Dr. Voeus said Luther 'was not called to be conferred with, or to disputation'
The chancellor of Trier dismissed Luther: 'you have leave and licence to depart again with your safe-conduct'
Luther left Worms on 26 April at ten o'clock
Sarpi: Luther departed 'the 26. of April'
Waterworth: 'Luther left Worms on the twenty-sixth of April'
The Edict carries out 'des decrets, Sentenz und verdamnus laut der bullen' and declares Luther 'als von gots kirchen abgesündert gelide und einen verstopten zertrenner und offenbarn ketzer'
After twenty days ending 14 May, no one is to 'hauset, hoffet, etzt, drenket, noch enthaltet' Luther; he is to be taken and sent to the emperor
The Edict orders action against Luther's 'mitverwandten, anhengern, enthaltern, fürschiebern, gönnern und nachvolgern' and their goods
Sarpi's summary of the Edict: Luther's books to be burned, and printing controlled
Waterworth: his writings to be seized and burnt, and works on the faith approved by the Ordinary before publication
Pallavicino: Aleander was charged to draw up the ban, and it was then revised in the emperor's councils
Five of Frederick's nobles in disguise stopped the carriage, took Luther 'con simulata forza', and brought him by night to the Wartburg; Frederick did not know which castle held him
Masked horsemen beat the drivers, made a show of violence and carried Luther to the Wartburg
Frederick 'conveyed Luther a little out of sight secretly'
Herrnschmid: Luther was seized on the road by horsemen and carried to a castle
Steimle: Luther entered the Wartburg on 4 May 1521
Frederick brought Luther to safety 'by means of a stratagem'
The Edict 'found, in general, no responsive reception' in Germany
Waterworth: Charles's departure and the elector's authority 'rendered the Ban ineffectual'
Luther, 1530: the decree was so horrible 'it had to be changed at the diet at Nuremberg'
Luther's Table Talk: the tyrants 'were constrained to recall the same again'
Luther, 1525: the synod at Buxtehude had Leo's bull and the imperial edict issued at Worms posted up against Friar Henry
The Council of Regency, by edict of 20 January 1522, demanded the Edict be carried out
At Speyer in 1526 Ferdinand announced the emperor's resolve to carry out the edict passed at Worms
The Augsburg decree of 1530 announced the emperor's resolve 'to carry out unconditionally the Edict of Worms'
The Edict's date of 8 May matches an alliance of emperor and pope 'to have the same friends and without exception the same enemies'
By the decree 'the emperor procured no small thanks with the pope'
Buchheim: the Peasants' Twelve Articles echo Luther's declaration at Worms
At the Wartburg Luther worked at 'the great work of his life, the translation of the Bible from the original text'
Buchheim calls Luther's refusal 'the official proclamation of the Reformation'
Waterworth tells Worms in his introduction to the Council of Trent
Melanchthon was at Wittenberg during the Wartburg months, so is not on the Who click
Herrnschmid: Luther 'added these German words, Hier stehe ich: ich kan nicht anders: Gott helfe mir! Amen.' (held OCR 'Hier flehe ich'; his name, l.3492, as 'Hernnfehmid')
Carlyle, quoted by Bacon: 'Here I stand - I cannot do otherwise - God be my help, Amen.'
Zinzendorf gives Luther's mind at Worms as 'da stehe ich, ich kan nicht anders, GOtt helffe mir'
Bacon calls the tiles saying 'the famous saying imputed to Luther'
Luther's own account of the tiles: 'although in Worms there were as many devils as there are tiles on the houses, yet, God willing, I will go thither'
Luther, 1522: 'I could have started such a little game at Worms that even the emperor would not have been safe'
Buchheim calls Charles 'a bigoted Roman Catholic at heart' (Buchheim's side)

contested_claims.claim: Whether Luther said 'Here I stand', and in what words
contested_claims.sides: Held tellings that have it: Foxe's English, 'Hereupon I stand and rest' (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.22078-22079); Herrnschmid, giving the German as words Luther added (arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.9300-9311); Carlyle, quoted by Bacon (luther_hymns_bacon-allen.txt l.603-652); Zinzendorf (zinzendorf_sammlung-oeffentlicher-reden-pennsylvania-deu_buedingen1746.txt l.30869-30872). Held tellings without it: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10076-10135), Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9625-9680), Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1726-1808) and Buchheim (luther_first-principles-reformation_wace-buchheim1885.txt l.2460-2475). Luther's Table Talk tells no speech of the second hearing; its 'next day' is the talks with 'the Bishops and others' (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3563-3565). No held editor discusses whether he said it.

contested_claims.claim: Who the Johann Eck who questioned Luther was
contested_claims.sides: The Leipzig opponent, 'John Eckius above mentioned', then the Trier official: Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.21752-21753). 'Another' Johann Eck, vicar of the archbishop of Trier: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10015-10017). 'The Bishop of Trier's fiscal', without more: Luther's Table Talk (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3551).

contested_claims.claim: How soon after his arrival the first hearing came
contested_claims.sides: The day after: Pallavicino, 17 April (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10012-10014); Waterworth, arrived 16 April and appeared on the 17th (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1724-1727); Herrnschmid, 'April 16. The next day' (arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.9150-9151). Sarpi gives 17 April for the hearing but no date for the arrival (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9617). The fourth day after: Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.21734), who gives no calendar date for either hearing.

contested_claims.claim: Twenty or twenty-one days for Luther's journey home
contested_claims.sides: Twenty-one: Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.22456-22458, 22484-22485), Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9707-9708), Sleidan as reported by Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1811). Twenty: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10357), Waterworth after him (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1803-1804), and the Edict's twenty days ending 14 May (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15612-15613, 15620).

contested_claims.claim: The Edict's date and the day it was signed
contested_claims.sides: Dated 8 May, signed by Charles on 26 May: Mirbt, from Wrede (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15590-15591). Signed in church on Trinity Sunday, 26 May, with the signature dated back to the eighth: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10500-10510). Put out on 25 May and post-dated to 8 May: Buchheim (luther_first-principles-reformation_wace-buchheim1885.txt l.2518-2521). Placed under the ban on 8 May: Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1831-1832). '8. of April': Sarpi's English (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.9712-9713), apparently a slip.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Diet consented to the Edict
contested_claims.sides: Yes: the Edict's own claim of 'einhelligem rat und willen' of electors, princes and estates (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15598-15600). Pallavicino says the whole Diet agreed with Charles's sentence, and Brandenburg answered for all that the ban pleased them (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10181, 10494-10500). Also Waterworth, 'with the consent of the Germanic Diet' (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1831-1833). No: Buchheim, 'without the formal sanction of the Diet', after Frederick and the Palatine had left (luther_first-principles-reformation_wace-buchheim1885.txt l.2509-2521).

contested_claims.claim: The date of Decet Romanum pontificem
contested_claims.sides: 2 January 1521: Mirbt (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15394). 3 January 1521: Luther's 1930 editors (luther_works-v3-selected_various1930.txt l.288-289) and Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.1659-1660).

contested_claims.claim: Who drafted the Edict
contested_claims.sides: Aleander drew up its content, and it was then revised in the emperor's councils: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.10448-10454). Herrnschmid seems to say it was drawn up by Aleander, but the OCR is broken (arminian-magazine_vol-1_1778.txt l.9403-9405). No held source names another drafter, and none confirms Pallavicino independently.

contested_claims.claim: Where Luther stood for his hearing
contested_claims.sides: 'The Senate House': Luther's Table Talk (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3547). 'The earl palatine's palace': Foxe (foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt l.21743-21744).

contested_claims.claim: How many grievances the estates brought
contested_claims.sides: 'Four hundred articles': Luther's Table Talk (luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt l.3530-3531). 'Some hundred and four statements': Luther in 1530 (luther_works-v4-selected_various1931.txt l.16043-16045). Mirbt prints only an excerpt (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15525-15580), so no count can be taken from it.

absent_details.note: Held only as Mirbt's excerpt of the German text from the Reichstagsakten (mirbt l.15586-15637). The parts on books and printing are known only from Sarpi's and Waterworth's summaries. The full Edict is named in the CFT-Wants Era 7 row for Worms.

absent_details.note: Not held. Searched cic/texts for 'descendu des', 'tres chrestiens empereurs', 'roys catholiques', 'Kaiser Karl', 'Karls V' and 'Carolus' near Worms. claims.claim: The reading took place on Saturday 25 June 1530 at 3 p.m.
The confession was presented on 25 June 1530
The reading was in the chapter hall of the bishop's palace, where the emperor lodged
The two Saxon chancellors Brück and Beyer stepped into the middle of the room, one with the German and one with the Latin copy
German was chosen after the elector of Saxony recalled that they were on German soil
Beyer read the German text
The reading took two hours, and it is said that everyone in the palace courtyard understood every word
Sarpi says the princes were before the emperor in a hall holding about 200, and the confession was read with a loud voice
The legate was absent on the day the confession was read
Both copies were signed before the reading
Charles kept the Latin copy, gave the German to the elector of Mainz for the imperial archive, and forbade publication
The princes were asked whether they dissented in anything more and answered that the document contained all they dissented from
The confession's preface, conclusion and signers are held in English and Swedish
The Catholic reply's content reaches us through Melanchthon, who says he worked from notes taken during the reading
Bensow edited the Swedish church's confessional books, with the Uppsala decisions of 1593, in 1912
Charles summoned the Diet on the Turk and on dissensions in religion. The parties' opinions were to be heard in each other's presence
The Tetrapolitan's preface says Charles sought to settle the grave and harmful religious split that had troubled Germany for some years
At Speyer in 1529 Charles had promised Clement VII to restore unity in the church
Charles's first plan was a general council, which the pope firmly opposed
Needing help against the Turks, Charles invited the estates in very conciliatory words
At Bologna Charles resolved to enforce the Edict of Worms and reduce the Lutherans to the unity of the Church
Charles left Bologna resolved that the separated princes should return to the obedience of the Church of Rome
Buchheim quotes the writ's aim 'to settle the prevailing discord' and holds that eradicating German 'heresy' was a principal motive
Clement VII instructed Vergerius to work that there should be no disputation in the Diet nor a council called in Germany
The Lutheran princes had appealed to a general, free Christian council and still adhered to the appeal
The confession asks only that the bishops allow the Gospel to be purely taught and relax some few observances
Hinke says neither Catholics nor Lutherans would have anything to do with the Reformed, quoting Bucer to Zwingli of 23 June
Charles V summoned the Diet at Augsburg
The Diet was summoned for 8 April 1530
The elector of Saxony arrived in Augsburg on 2 May and waited over six weeks for the emperor
The confession's princes say they came promptly and were among the first at Augsburg
The emperor arrived on 15 June, the eve of Corpus Christi
Waterworth alone says the Diet opened on 20 June with the emperor's speech
The Confutation was read on 3 August
The final decree is dated 19 November 1530
Waterworth says the decree was published on 22 November
Pallavicino says the Diet met with an unusual attendance of princes, church and lay
The emperor came with the legate Campeggio and a large retinue of princes, ambassadors and electors
The confession is signed by seven princes and the senates of Nuremberg and Reutlingen
The decree names the elector of Saxony, five princes and six cities
Bossert's note lists the decree's princes and the cities Nuremberg, Reutlingen, Kempten, Heilbronn, Windsheim and Weissenburg
The elector brought Luther, Melanchthon, Spalatin, Justus Jonas and Agricola
Bensow names Jonas, Agricola, Spalatin, Schnepf and Brenz as the theologians at Augsburg, with Brück
Waterworth names Faber, Eck and Cochlaeus as the most distinguished of the reply's writers
Bucer and Capito drew up the Tetrapolitan
Waterworth says Bucer and Capito presented it; its title says the four cities' envoys did
Jacob Sturm sent Zwingli a copy of the Augsburg Confession on 31 May
Vadian was at Augsburg during the Diet and corresponded with Zwingli
Pallavicino names seven a side for the talks. His Catholics are the bishop of Augsburg, a duke of Brunswick later replaced by Duke George of Saxony, two chancellors, Eck, Wimpina and a third
Pallavicino names for the Lutherans John Frederick, George of Brandenburg, Gregor Brück, 'D. Heller', Melanchthon, Brenz and Schnepf
The day after the reading the Catholic members, with the legate and many theologians, resolved to have a refutation drawn up
The Catholic estates gave the task to Campeggio, who gave it to about twenty theologians
Waterworth says the reply was completed on 13 July and required to be made shorter and less violent
Bensow dates the first draft to 12 July and says the emperor was angered by it
Alexander Schweiss read the reply on 3 August in the same room as the confession
The reply was accepted by the emperor as his own
The Lutherans called the Catholic reply the confutatio
Melanchthon says the emperor demanded the princes assent to the confutation and they could get a copy only on perilous conditions
The terms of 5 August: a copy if they made no reply, showed it to no one and did not print it
Pallavicino gives the imperial reason for withholding the copy: the preachers had mocked the Edict of Worms
Melanchthon: 'how could they assent to a writing into which they had not looked?'
A commission of seven a side was formed, later three a side
Sarpi says some few small points were agreed but no concord
Pallavicino says agreement was on the most important articles
Zwingli's Account of the Faith was handed to the emperor on 8 July
The Tetrapolitan was handed to the emperor on 11 July
Zwingli signed his Account at Zurich on 3 July
The emperor had the cities' writing answered and refused them a copy
Eck's refutation of Zwingli is dated Augsburg, 17 July 1530
Hinke judges the emperor probably never read a line of Zwingli's confession
Melanchthon says the Apology was offered and the emperor did not receive it
Brück handed over the Apology on 22 September; it is told that Ferdinand whispered to the emperor, who then refused it
Section 4 says the elector, five princes and six cities should join the emperor and the other estates against those who do not hold the sacrament and the Anabaptists
Section 40 keeps the law against the Anabaptists and orders children baptized with chrism
Waterworth gives the 22 September draft with a term to 15 April 1531, at least until a general council
Buchheim says the decree of 19 November carried the 15 April 1531 term
A council was to be called within six months and held within a year
Waterworth says the final form proscribed the Zwinglians, degraded married priests, rebuilt monasteries and promised a council
The Protestant princes opposed the September draft edict except the clauses against the Anabaptists and Zwinglians, and refused aid against the Turk
In the Apology Melanchthon writes that 'a horrible decree' has been prepared against them; H. E. Jacobs's note identifies it as the recess of 19 November

claims.claim: The princes met at Smalcald on 22 December and signed a treaty for mutual defense. Its form was drawn up on 31 December and signed on 4 January 1531
The Smalcald League was formed in December 1530 and even Luther approved
Clement VII was grieved that the emperor received confessions and held talks, and above all by the promised council
Waterworth says the events at Augsburg confirmed the emperor's hope in a general council
The estates endorsed the Apology at Schweinfurt in 1532, and all the theologians at Smalcald signed it in 1537
The 1580 preface roots the Book of Concord in the confession offered at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530
The Formula of Concord says the Zwinglian teachers separated when the confession was presented

claims.claim: Gilles dates the general assembly at Angrogne to 12 September 1532
Morland heads the confession 'assembled in Angrogne the 12. of September of the Year 1532'
Muston dates the synodal assembly at Angrogna to 12 September 1532 and says it lasted six days
Montet dates the synod of Angrogne to 12 September 1532
Zezschwitz dates the synod of Angrogne to 12 September 1532 and places 'die Synode zu Chanforans im Thale von Angrogne' in 1532
Perrin dates the assembly at Angrogne to 12 September 1535, in the French and in the English
Perrin dates the barbes' resolve to preach the Gospel openly to 1532, before his 1535 assembly
Léger's heading, as the OCR reads, dates the confession to '1 1. de Décembre 1531'. He says his copy is kept at Cambridge
Montet's quotation of the manuscript reads 'en Angroma l'anno del Segnor 1533, e a di 12 de septembro' (OCR 'Vanno', 'septemhro'), against his own 1532
A prisoner in Bersour's inquiry said the barbes had then ('alors') held their synod, which lasted six days; Gilles adds that the Latin trial record calls it 'Capitulum'
Muston places the meeting in the open air at the hamlet of Chanforans in the commune of Angrogna
Muston quotes the manuscript: 'En presencia de tuti li ministri et eciam Dio del populo' (OCR 'Bio'). He cites it as 'MS. of George Morel, Dublin, C, V, No. 18'
Montet quotes the manuscript: 'en presentia di tuti li ministri e eciam dio del populo', and its first question, whether a Christian may lawfully swear
Montet calls the manuscript 'les actes du Synode d'Angrogne' and says it is written in a dialect close to Italian
Muston calls the manuscript 'the contemporary manuscript'
Gilles says the conclusions were fully proved 'par les actes et manuscrit qui en fut dressé', and calls his own list 'en substance le principal'
Perrin says the Waldensians sent two barbes, George Morel of Freissinières and Pierre Masson of Burgundy. They went to Oecolampadius at Basel, Capito and Bucer at Strasbourg and Haller at Berne
The Histoire ecclésiastique attributed to Beza gives the same deputation of Morel and Masson to Basel, Strasbourg and Berne
Morland dates the mission to 1530 and says Masson was taken prisoner at Dijon
Montet dates the barbes' contact with the reformers to 1530
Morel wrote to Oecolampadius: 'pauures instructeurs de ce petit peuple, auons demeuré plus de quatre cens ans parmi des cruelles espines' (long s normalized)
Oecolampadius wrote in 1530: 'la peur d'estre persecutés vous fait dissimuler en vostre foy & que vous la cachés' (long s normalized)
Oecolampadius wrote that going to 'leurs Messes abominables' they heard blasphemies against Christ's death and passion
Gilles sums up the reformers' advice in three heads. Settle disputed points of doctrine; hold church order and assemblies more openly; bar members from the Mass and Roman priests
Gilles says the matters were debated in the valleys and that pastors from the reformers' lands came to help before the assembly
Gilles says each side had time and liberty to propose and answer
Gilles says some barbes judged the new rules 'pas totalement nécessaires', that they shamed the memory of earlier leaders, and that openness would provoke persecution
Gilles says only 'fut convoquée une Assemblée générale en Angrogne', naming no convener
Perrin says they gathered from all their valleys so that all might be done in order, naming no convener
Perrin: 'tous les chefs de famille auec leurs Pasteurs', from all their valleys
Morland: 'the Ministers, and Heads of Families of the Churches of the Valleys of Piemont'
Gilles: 'des Pasteurs, et principaux des Eglises Vaudoises, tant des Valées, que des pays circonvoisins'
Muston has representatives from Calabria, Saluces, Provence and Dauphiny
Muston has the seigneurs of Miradol, Rivenoble and Solaro appear, citing no witness

Jeanet Peiret of Angrogna, a guard Bersour caught, testified on 22 September. He said they kept guard for the ministers 'assemblez en la bourgade des Chanforans au milieu d'Angrogne' (Gilles places the watch in 1535: Peiret was one of those Bersour caught keeping guard)

Peiret said that among them was 'M. Farel, qui avoit la barbe rouge, et un beau cheval blanc', with two companions (the 1881 OCR reads 'Farel.'; the 1644 print has the comma) (Gilles places the watch in 1535)
Gilles says these were 'des Pasteurs qui continuoyent de venir des quartiers de Suisse'
Gilles places Peiret's deposition in Bersour's inquiry, after the duke's patents of 28 August 1535
Muston puts Farel, on a white horse, and Saulnier at the 1532 meeting
Baum and Cunitz, citing Herminjard, say Olivetan visited the valleys with Farel and Saunier in 1532. There, they say, he received the charge to translate the Bible
Muston quotes Olivetan's 'Apologie du translateur' as the words of 'one who was present at that meeting'
Perrin and Morland say the articles were signed and sworn by all present
Muston says the declaration was signed by the greater part, and two pastors refused to sign, citing Gilles
Perrin says one of the assembly reported on Morel and Masson's mission, and the letters of Oecolampadius and Bucer were read
Perrin says the articles were 'dressés, leus, approuués, signés, & iuré par tous les assistans' (OCR 'drefies', 'fignés')
Perrin, Morland and Léger print the same seventeen articles in the same order
Article 1: divine service can only be done in spirit and in truth
Article 2: all who have been and shall be saved were elected of God before the foundation of the world
Article 3: 'It is impossible that those that are appointed to salvation, should not be saved' (long s normalized)
Article 4: whoever upholds free will denies predestination and the grace of God
Article 6: a Christian may swear by the name of God
Article 7: auricular confession is not commanded of God
Article 10: a Christian may exercise the office of magistrate over Christians
Articles 12 and 13: marriage is forbidden to none, and whoever forbids it teaches a diabolical doctrine
Article 16: ministers may own some estate to keep their families
Article 17: only two sacramental signs, baptism and the Eucharist
Gilles says the assembly resolved to reject all dissimulation and take no further part in the ceremonies of the Roman Church
Muston says the manuscript's first question concerned oaths
Muston says the manuscript has struck-out items on Sunday work, the laying on of hands and usury
Muston gives the manuscript's articles XVIII to XXIII
Muston quotes the closing declaration: 'nothing may henceforth divide us'
Perrin says that after the articles 'ils se resolurent de faire imprimer promptement toute la Bible' (OCR 'pro. ptément')
Muston says the synod resolved on the Bible, citing Olivetan's 'Apologie du translateur'
Perrin says the priests there for the parish revenues saw 'la porte fermee à leur gain'. 'Ils se retirerent sans sonner mot', and the Mass 'se bannit d'elle mesme des vallees' (long s normalized)
Gilles names Daniel de Valence and Jean de Molines, 'venus de dehors des Valées', who 'partirent sans congé de l'assemblée' and went to Bohemia
Gilles says the two complained of innovations brought in by ministers 'venus d'Alemagne', given entry too easily
Blahoslav's Summa (1556): two learned Frenchmen came from the Waldensians and told of 'quandam mutationem atque dissidium seu discordiam exortam'
Blahoslav: the two stayed 'per integrum semestre unum', praised all they saw and returned to their own in France
Goll's note identifies the two envoys as Daniel von Valence and Johannes von Molines
Comenius has two Frenchmen sent by the Waldensian brethren stay six whole months
Perrin says Valence and Molines were sent to serve the Bohemian churches and betrayed them to their enemies
Morland says the two were sent into Bohemia by the other barbes and shamefully betrayed those churches
Léger says the two were sent to Bohemia and through 'une trop grande imprudence' revealed those churches to their enemies
Gilles says the Bohemian pastors wrote on 27 June 1533 (1644 OCR reads '17.de Iuin')
Gilles says the Bohemian letter speaks only honorably of the two barbes
Gilles places the next assembly in Val S. Martin on 15 August 1533, which confirmed 'la conclusion faite l'année précédente en Angrogne'
Montet places the confirming synod at Saint-Martin on 15 August 1533
Muston places the next synod at Pral on 14 August 1533
Gilles says the two then withdrew to live on their own and carried off what they could of the old Waldensian manuscripts
Gilles says persecution and war let the decisions be carried out only 'avec une assez longue suite de temps'
Gilles dates the duke's patents to Bersour to 28 August 1535
Morland says the valleys in 1535 had the first French Bible printed at their own cost, through their interpreter Robert Olivetan
Morland lists the French Bible printed by the valleys at Neuchâtel in 1535 among the volumes he deposited
Perrin says they gave fifteen hundred gold crowns to a printer at Neuchâtel for the first French Bible seen in France
Léger says Olivetan translated and printed the Bible at Neuchâtel at the valleys' cost (the year is unclear in the OCR)
The Histoire ecclésiastique says they had the first French Bible printed at Neuchâtel at their own cost (OCR 'i635'). Olivetan translated it with Calvin's help
Muston gives the preface's date, 7 February 1535, and the colophon: Neuchâtel, Pierre de Wingle, 4 June 1535; the cost 1500 golden crowns
Baum and Cunitz date Pierre de Wingle's printing at Neuchâtel to 4 June 1535
Olivetan's preface says 'un certain pauure peuple' gave him the charge. He was to draw 'iceluy thresor hors des armaires & coffres Ebraicques & Grecz' (OCR normalized)
Morland says the Bible was printed 'for the benefit of the Evangelical Churches where this Language was in use'
Léger quotes Beza: through the Waldensians of the valleys France has the Bible in its own language

Léger, on the Waldensians' talks with the reformers: 'Je ne trouve point qu'ils y ayent changé la moindre chose'. The exception is their near-Anabaptist view that only magistrates should wield the sword, which they still held in 1560, in Emanuel Philibert's war, and acted otherwise only later, after the Maccabees' example
Montet: 'La doctrine protestante était en fait une nouveauté pour les Vaudois'
Montet dates the absolute and final triumph of Protestantism among the Waldensians to the Union of the Valleys of 11 November 1571
Gilles says the churches joined the other Reformed churches 'environ l'année 1530'

Zezschwitz says Morel, 'noch 1532', voiced his churches' surprise at Luther's teaching on the bound will; the held letters date Morel's mission to 1530 (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.14262-14271; morland_history-evangelical-churches-piemont_1658.txt l.21825-21826). The 1532 decrees, he says, breathe the firmest predestinarian teaching
Perrin lists Valence and Molines under Provence
Léger gives Molines as 'de la Vallée de Queyras'
Muston says the two dissenting pastors belonged to Dauphiny
Gilles says some barbes did not consent to all the conclusions, and names Daniel de Valence and Jean de Molines as two of the leading objectors ('deux des principaux contredisans')
Blahoslav: the envoys said they were sent by the Waldensian community ('missos esse a coetu Waldensium'), to see whether the Unity had changed and its ministers married

Crespin's editors (Benoît and Lelièvre, 1885), after Merle d'Aubigné and Herminjard: Martin Gonin came with another barbe to invite Farel and Saunier, then at Grandson, to the synod of Angrogne held on 12 September (the OCR year reads 1552; Gonin left Geneva in April 1536 and was then taken prisoner, l.49944-49962)

Also Morland (morland_history-evangelical-churches-piemont_1658.txt l.7939-7942). Also Muston (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6408-6410). Also Montet (montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.939-941; montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.9124-9126). Also Zezschwitz (zezschwitz_katechismen-der-waldenser-und-boehmischen-brueder-deu_1863.txt l.6309-6311). 12 September 1535: Perrin (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.11970-11974; perrin_history-ancient-christians-valleys-alps_1847.txt l.5263-5265). 11 December 1531, as the OCR reads: Léger (leger_histoire-generale-eglises-vaudoises-livre1-fra_1669.txt l.13065-13067). 1533 in Montet's quotation of the manuscript, against his own 1532 (montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.979-980). No held writer discusses Perrin's 1535.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the name Chanforans and Farel's presence belong to the 1532 meeting
contested_claims.sides: The only witness of the time is Peiret's deposition, which Gilles places in Bersour's inquiry of 1535 (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2328-2330; gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2441-2451). Gilles has Peiret caught on watch, for ministers then gathered (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2441-2445), and the prisoner's synod 'alors' (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2464-2466). Gilles names no visitor at the 1532 assembly (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.1911-1918) and says the Swiss pastors 'continuoyent de venir' (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2450-2451). Tied to 1532: Muston (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6382-6384; muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6402-6410; muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.7484-7485), Baum and Cunitz from Herminjard (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.2433-2435), Crespin's editors, after Merle d'Aubigné and Herminjard: Gonin and another barbe invited Farel and Saunier from Grandson to the synod of 12 September (crespin_histoire-des-martyrs-t1-fra_benoit-lelievre1885.txt l.49905-49911), Zezschwitz for the name (zezschwitz_katechismen-der-waldenser-und-boehmischen-brueder-deu_1863.txt l.11544-11546).

contested_claims.claim: What the two dissenting barbes did and how they parted
contested_claims.sides: Walked out of the assembly in protest and took their complaint to Bohemia: Gilles (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2047-2058). Sent by the barbes to Bohemia and betrayed its churches: Perrin (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.6538-6550; perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.14672-14680). So also Morland (morland_history-evangelical-churches-piemont_1658.txt l.21810-21820), Léger, by 'trop grande imprudence' (leger_histoire-generale-eglises-vaudoises-livre1-fra_1669.txt l.22897-22900). Came as envoys sent by the Waldensians, told of discord at home, stayed six months and left on good terms: Blahoslav (goll_quellen-bohmische-bruder-v1-deu_1878.txt l.7159-7183), with Goll's identification (goll_quellen-bohmische-bruder-v1-deu_1878.txt l.7223-7224); Comenius (comenius_historia-fratrum-bohemorum-lat_1702.txt l.2805-2816). The Bohemian letter, as Gilles gives it, has them say they were sent (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2066-2067). Gilles says the Bohemian letter blames them for nothing (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2145-2148).

contested_claims.claim: That the Waldensians joined the Reformation in 1532, and what the meeting changed
contested_claims.sides: About 1530: Gilles's preface (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.238-241). Nothing changed in their dealings with the reformers; their near-Anabaptist view that only magistrates bear the sword held until at least 1560, in Emanuel Philibert's war, and only later, after the Maccabees' example, did they act otherwise: Léger (leger_histoire-generale-eglises-vaudoises-livre1-fra_1669.txt l.23072-23086). Protestant teaching a novelty, its full triumph in 1571: Montet (montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.9213-9219; montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.9165-9170). The 1532 decrees firmly predestinarian, against Morel's earlier unease: Zezschwitz (zezschwitz_katechismen-der-waldenser-und-boehmischen-brueder-deu_1863.txt l.6303-6311). Gilles says the reformers found 'quelques défauts' to remedy (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.1886-1888).

contested_claims.claim: The form of the articles: the printed seventeen or the manuscript
contested_claims.sides: Seventeen in the same order: Perrin (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.12019-12133), Morland (morland_history-evangelical-churches-piemont_1658.txt l.7952-8036), Léger (leger_histoire-generale-eglises-vaudoises-livre1-fra_1669.txt l.13070-13174). A summary of the main points: Gilles (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.1993-1997). At least twenty-three, with struck items: the manuscript as Muston describes it (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6452-6538); Montet's Italianate lines (montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.9141-9182). No held writer doubts the articles are genuine.

contested_claims.claim: Whether all present signed
contested_claims.sides: All present signed and swore: Perrin (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.12007-12012), Morland (morland_history-evangelical-churches-piemont_1658.txt l.7944-7946). The greater part signed and two refused: Muston, citing Gilles (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6538-6542). Gilles says the two left without leave and does not speak of signing (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2047-2052). Gilles says some barbes did not consent to all the conclusions (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2030-2031); Montet: 'une faible minorité' (montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.9152); Zezschwitz: two leaders of the minority left (zezschwitz_katechismen-der-waldenser-und-boehmischen-brueder-deu_1863.txt l.11554-11555).

contested_claims.claim: The place and day of the assembly of 1533
contested_claims.sides: Val S. Martin, 15 August 1533: Gilles (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2153-2154), Montet (montet_histoire-litteraire-des-vaudois-du-piemont-fra_1885.txt l.9152-9155). Pral, 14 August 1533: Muston (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6571-6572). Pral lies in Val San Martino; the day differs.

contested_claims.claim: Where the dissenting barbes came from
contested_claims.sides: From outside the valleys: Gilles (gilles_histoire-ecclesiastique-eglises-vaudoises-v1-fra_1881.txt l.2047-2049). Dauphiny: Muston (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6545-6547). Listed under Provence: Perrin (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.6540-6541). Molines of the Queyras valley: Léger (leger_histoire-generale-eglises-vaudoises-livre1-fra_1669.txt l.22894-22896).

contested_claims.claim: When the decision to print the Bible was made
contested_claims.sides: After the articles, at the assembly Perrin dates 1535: Perrin (perrin_histoire-des-vaudois-fra_1619.txt l.12154-12158). At the 1532 synod: Muston, from Olivetan's unheld apology (muston_israel-of-the-alps-v1_montgomery1866.txt l.6436-6441). Olivetan received the charge in the valleys in 1532: Baum and Cunitz (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.2433-2435).

absent_details.detail: Who called the assembly
absent_details.note: No held line names a convener. Gilles has only 'fut convoquée une Assemblée générale' (gilles 1881 l.1914). Perrin has 'ils s'assemblerent de toutes leurs vallees' (perrin 1619 l.11971-11972). Muston has 'a synod was held' (l.6379). Passages read whole in Perrin 1619, Perrin 1847, Gilles 1644 and 1881, Morland, Léger and Muston.

absent_details.detail: A count of those present
absent_details.note: None held. Read whole the assembly passages in Perrin (both), Gilles, Morland, Léger, Muston and Montet. Searched cent|hundred|nombre|number and two- or three-digit numbers near them. Perrin and Morland say only 'all present'.

absent_details.detail: A signed list of names
absent_details.note: Not held. Perrin and Morland say the articles were signed but print no names. Searched fign|sign|subscri|soubsign|liste|noms around the passages in Perrin 1619, Morland, Léger and Gilles 1881.

absent_details.detail: The original manuscript of the propositions
absent_details.note: Not held. Known only through quotations by Muston (l.6392-6393, 6450-6538) and Montet (l.979-981, 9141-9182). Léger's copy was at Cambridge (l.13067-13068); not held.

absent_details.detail: The dissenting barbes' own words
absent_details.note: No writing by Daniel de Valence or Jean de Molines is held. Searched all of cic/texts for Valence|Valentia|Valenza|Valencia with Molin, and both names in Gilles, Perrin, Léger, Morland, Goll, Comenius and Zezschwitz. Their case reaches us through Gilles and through the Brethren's chronicle.

absent_details.detail: A witness of the time placing Saunier or Olivetan at the 1532 meeting
absent_details.note: None held. Muston (l.6404-6405, 6411-6412), the Baum and Cunitz note from Herminjard (beza t1 l.2433-2435) and Crespin's editors (crespin t1 l.49905-49911) say so; Herminjard and Merle d'Aubigné are not held. A 1539 letter of Libertet to Farel says Olivetan went to the Waldensians with Farel, without a date (calvin opera vol10 l.48140-48141).

absent_details.detail: The Olivetan Bible itself and its 'Apologie du translateur'
absent_details.note: Not held. Only the preface is held, in Morland (l.5764-6030) and in part in Léger (l.19325-19345). Muston's account of the synod's Bible decision rests on the unheld apology (l.6440-6441).

absent_details.detail: Oecolampadius's letter in its original Latin
absent_details.note: Held only in Perrin's French (l.5482-5540, 14259-14320) and English (perrin 1847 l.2688-2714). Scultetus, Montet's source, is not held (montet l.9002-9004).

absent_details.detail: A held line that Farel 'pressed the union' at the assembly
absent_details.note: None found. The census's voice line for the Waldensian-Reformed Union says so. The held witnesses place Farel among the ministers (gilles 1881 l.2446-2448; muston l.6402-6405) and say the Bible 'originated through the influence of Farel' (muston l.6626). Searched Farel in Gilles, Perrin, Morland, Léger, Muston and Montet.
